title: Réti against Tartakower, Vienna 1910: a queen sacrifice and a mate in three

game.score_checked: 21 plies; every move legal in python-chess; ends in checkmate (11.Bd8#); the full record is identical in Winter's article and a second page; see the sources

outcomes: Predicts the key moves of a famous game from the positions, with no idea named
Names the check that attacks the king twice at once and says why the king could only move
Says which moment of the game they would have missed, and what they would have needed to notice

steps.text: **Vienna, 1910.** Richard Réti had White against Savielly Tartakower. The score is a Caro-Kann Defense. Sources differ on whether it was a tournament game or a casual one. The moves below agree in two independent sources. You will play White at five moments, with no hint about which idea decides each. Engine remarks say *the engine at depth 16*: a rating at that search depth, not a proof.

steps.caption: The first six moves of each side, ending with a check on White's king. Step through them.

line.say: Black pushes the d-pawn to attack the pawn on e4.
Black takes the pawn on e4.
Black pushes the e-pawn to challenge d4.
White takes the pawn on e5.
The queen checks the king along the diagonal a5-e1.

claims.statement: After 6...Qa5+ one black piece attacks White's king on e1.

steps.caption: White blocked the check. What Black did next.

line.say: The bishop blocks the check and comes into the game.
Black takes the pawn on e5; the queen now attacks the knight on e4.

claims.statement: After 7...Qxe5 two black pieces attack the knight on e4.
One white piece defends the knight on e4, the queen on d3.

steps.caption: White castled. What Black did next.

line.say: The king goes to c1 and the rook to d1.
Black takes the knight on e4, which the white queen defended. The knight now attacks the bishop on d2.

claims.statement: After 8...Nxe4 one black piece attacks the bishop on d2.

steps.caption: After 9.Qd8+ the queen stands on d8 with check. Is Black's reply a choice?

line.say: The king takes the queen. It is the only legal reply.

claims.statement: Black's king is in check from the queen on d8.
Kxd8 is Black's only legal move.

steps.caption: After 10.Bg5+ two pieces check the king on d8, the bishop and the rook. The king has two legal squares; the game went to c7.

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack the king on d8.
The king can go only to c7 or e8.

line.say: Bd8 is checkmate: the rook defends the bishop, and Black's own knight and bishop block b8 and c8.

steps.text: **Skills at work, not re-taught here.** *Mating patterns* (the final mate with a bishop defended by a rook), *Double check* and *Discovered attacks and checks* (10.Bg5+), *Types of sacrifice* (the queen given up for mate), *Searching for a forced mate* (all three finishing moves were checks). Our reading: move 8 prepared it, because castling put the rook on d1 behind its own bishop and queen. That is a reading of the position, not a claim about what either player thought.

steps.prompt: Which of the five moments (7.Bd2, 8.O-O-O, 9.Qd8+, 10.Bg5+, 11.Bd8#) would you have missed in a game of your own, and what would you have had to notice?

fields.label: The moment I would have missed:
What I would have needed to notice:
options: a check that leaves one reply
a piece that blocks its own rook
a file that opens when a piece moves
the king's own pieces blocking it
